source.title: KV Shifting Attention Enhances Language Modeling
source.authors: Mingyu Xu; Wei Cheng; Bingning Wang; Weipeng Chen

page_placements.theme: Architectural changes that build in or reroute induction (KV shifting, convolution, n-gram heads, value residuals)

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some cited figures are not rendered with their plotted values in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study gives theoretical constructions and synthetic-task induction-accuracy experiments, using methods and measures different from the original sources’ mechanistic and training-dynamics analyses.
record.gate_note: The study directly analyzes induction-head representation and reports toy-task induction accuracy. Its large-model language-modeling losses, benchmark scores, few-shot MMLU results, n-gram task, and math results do not measure induction behavior or token-index ICL loss, so they are not rows for these claim versions. Figure 1’s plotted values are unavailable in the supplied text; only the authors’ textual descriptions can be recorded.
record.test_reason: The study is mainly an architecture proposal. Its vanilla-transformer toy runs bear weakly on V1: on synthetic [A][B]…[A] data, a one-layer model struggles and a two-layer model learns induction. That depth pattern fits the cross-layer composition V1 describes. The study does not trace previous-token heads or composition. Its models are Llama-style with MLPs, not attention-only.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that KV shifting lowers the depth and width needed for induction heads and speeds induction learning on toy tasks. They also say it improves language modeling at 1.5B–19B scale, which they take as implicit evidence that learning induction heads matters for language modeling. They give no direct mechanistic evidence for that last link.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes attention by mixing shifted keys and values and evaluates induction accuracy on synthetic sequences; it does not reproduce the original mechanistic tracing or ICL loss-by-token-index measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The toy results vary with model depth and hidden size. The paper reports faster induction learning for one-layer KV shifting than two-layer vanilla at hidden size 1024, and poor performance for two-layer vanilla at hidden size 8.

fits_no_version.finding: A one-layer KV-shifting attention can exactly represent the induction function (Theorem 2). A one-layer KV-shifting model learns synthetic induction faster than a two-layer vanilla model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixing keys and values from adjacent tokens lets induction be implemented in a single attention layer, removing the need for previous-token-head composition.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 3 gradient-flow analysis of the KV-shifting parameters. With a small O(T) term, optimization may go through a small non-monotonic phase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning dynamics of induction in modified attention.

record.code_released: Training and inference implementation is included in Appendix F; no code URL is stated. The paper links pretrained models at https://huggingface.co/xumingyu16/Baseline_2.9B and https://huggingface.co/xumingyu16/KV_shifting_2.9B.
record.problems: The induction experiments are synthetic, and Figure 1’s numeric results are unavailable in the supplied text. The authors state that most experiments were run only once because of compute limits. Their large-model data are private, and the paper does not empirically trace induction-head circuits in the pretrained models.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for large-model training-loss curves, benchmark scores, few-shot MMLU, n-gram, ablation, multi-hop, or math results: these do not measure induction-head behavior or the claim’s token-index ICL measure. Figure 1 values unavailable from the supplied text are recorded as figure only rather than inferred.

untested.parts: No identification of a previous-token head, of K-composition, or of induction attention patterns. No attention-only models were used.
Not tested: no ICL score by token index, no loss bump, and no timing of formation in vanilla models.
Not tested. Large-model benchmark gains are only argued to 'implicitly' reflect induction.
Not tested. The seed and learning-rate runs report training loss only.
Not tested for standard transformers. The Theorem 3 dynamics concern KV-shifting parameters only.

missing.what: Numeric induction-accuracy curves over training for vanilla 1-, 2- and 4-layer and KV-shifting models, and for different widths. These values are not available in the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is mostly a method paper (closer to T4); only the vanilla baselines on the toy task bear on V1, and only behaviourally. The toy models include MLPs (Llama architecture), not attention-only, as the authors note in footnote 4. Most experiments were run once, and the large-model data are private.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not empirically identify or trace composition with an earlier previous-token head in a conventional attention-only model. Its toy experiments use a Llama-like architecture; its theoretical results concern induction-function representation.
The paper measures synthetic-task induction accuracy during training, but does not measure later-token loss relative to earlier-token loss, a sharp ICL gain, or a corresponding training-loss bump.
The large-model language-modeling and few-shot benchmark results do not measure induction heads as the cause of most ICL or token-index loss changes.
The study does not test induction behavior across model families, modalities, or independent training runs. Its seed experiments report training loss, not induction behavior.
Learning-rate and seed experiments report language-model training loss, not whether or when induction heads form or whether ICL persists.
The study reports few-shot task scores but does not test whether task learning runs through mechanisms other than induction heads.

The paper discusses optimization dynamics for its KV-shifting parameters, including a possible small non-monotonic process, but does not test whether induction-head formation consists of multiple transitions.

rows.subject: two-layer single-head transformer (Theorem 1)
rows.operation_detail: Constructs a two-layer transformer without FFNs to approximate the defined induction-head machine.
rows.note: A constructive approximation result, not an empirical tracing of head composition.
rows.check: Cited result: Theorem 1 is modified from Wang et al. (2024). It is a constructive approximation bound, not a measurement of what trained models do. It should not be a result row.

rows.subject: one-layer single-head KV shifting attention (Theorem 2)
rows.operation_detail: Constructs a one-layer KV-shifting attention mechanism representing the defined induction-head machine.
rows.note: The result is a constructive representation claim for modified attention, not evidence that a conventional one-layer transformer learns induction.
rows.check: Representation result for the authors' own KV-shifting attention, not a standard transformer. It does not bear on the system V1 names; it is recorded under fits_no_version.

relation.reason: The study reports its own induction-task results with vanilla controls across architectural conditions, bearing on dependence on the training setup. Its language-modeling improvements alone do not establish induction heads' causal role.

tranche.reason: The controlled depth, width, and attention comparisons examine architecture-dependent induction learning by a different method, bearing on V5. They do not directly test V1's attention-only composition mechanism.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased: KV shifting improves toy induction learning and language modeling, with the latter offered as implicit evidence. The theorem uses infinite precision; footnote 3 cautions that the representation constructions are upper bounds, not comparative lower-bound proofs.

statements.correction: Section 3.2: hidden size 1024; one-layer vanilla has difficulty learning induction; two-layer vanilla learns induction perfectly; Llama-style architecture with MLPs; no mechanistic tracing of composition.
statements.problem: The cited depth contrast is present, but the text reports one-layer difficulty rather than categorical failure. These Llama-style models have MLPs, and the study does not trace the previous-token-head composition specified by V1.

statements.correction: Two-layer Llama-style vanilla transformer: poor induction learning at hidden size 8; perfect induction learning at hidden size 1024; no exact accuracies stated; evidence of architecture-dependent behavioral learning, without a direct V1 test.
statements.problem: The width comparison and qualitative outcomes are accurate, but they do not demonstrate a scope limitation of V1's attention-only composition mechanism.

statements.correction: Section 3.2: one-layer KV-shifting attention learns induction perfectly and converges much faster than two-layer vanilla; previous-token information is supplied through modified attention; no counterexample to composition in conventional attention-only transformers is established.
statements.problem: The faster learning of one-layer KV shifting is correctly reported. Its use as a qualification of V1 requires distinguishing modified attention from the attention-only transformer mechanism V1 specifies.
